source: Rudner (1953) The Scientist Qua Scientist Makes Value Judgments
finding: Core argument. Science accepts or rejects hypotheses. No hypothesis is fully verified. So the scientist must decide the evidence is strong enough. How strong is enough depends on how bad a mistake would be.
numbers: Six-page paper, no experiment. Two worked cases: toxic ingredient of a drug not lethal (needs very high confidence) vs lot of machine-stamped belt buckles not defective (needs much less).
quote: How sure we need to be before we accept a hypothesis will depend on how serious a mistake would be.
limits: A philosophical argument, not an empirical result. Written at the Naval Research Laboratory. Rudner says it is a rational reconstruction, not a description of what scientists do; that would need sociology and psychology of science.
agent_relevance: Direct ancestor of our rule: the acceptance threshold is a function of error cost, not a fixed number. The agent needs an explicit cost-of-error input per claim.

source: Rudner (1953) The Scientist Qua Scientist Makes Value Judgments (Manhattan Project example)
finding: Rudner asks what probability the Manhattan Project scientists demanded for 'no uncontrollable chain reaction', why that value, and whether the question was even raised consciously.
numbers: No numbers given. It is a question, not a finding.
limits: Illustrative only. Rudner says the point is general beyond quality control.
agent_relevance: Shows the worst case for a fixed threshold: catastrophic, irreversible error needs a threshold far above the default. A gate for irreversible actions fits the schema guardrails.

source: Rudner (1953) The Scientist Qua Scientist Makes Value Judgments (reply to the 'just report probabilities' objection)
finding: Rudner pre-empts the later Jeffrey reply. Saying 'the probability is p' is itself accepting the hypothesis that the probability is p. So the value decision is only moved, not removed.
quote: nothing more than the acceptance by the scientist of the hypothesis that the degree of confidence is p
limits: Jeffrey (1956) and Levi (1960) answered that this regress is blocked by confining science to probability statements or to epistemic values. Henschen (2021) argues defenders have not beaten those replies.
agent_relevance: Warns that a verbal confidence number is also a claim with its own error cost. Links to verbal-confidence and imprecise-credence subfields.

source: Rudner (1953) The Scientist Qua Scientist Makes Value Judgments (what to do about it)
finding: Rudner's remedy. Objectivity means being explicit about which value judgments are made, not hiding them. Making them intuitively, unconsciously or haphazardly leaves part of scientific method out of control.
quote: to make them intuitively, unconsciously, haphazardly, is to leave an essential aspect of scientific method scientifically out of control
limits: Rudner calls for a 'science of ethics' that he expects to take many generations.
agent_relevance: Supports a design rule: the cost-of-error assumption must be written down and visible, not left implicit in the model's tone. Fits the schema habit of code-checked, recorded decisions.

source: Hempel (1965) Science and Human Values, as quoted in Douglas (2000)
finding: Hempel coined 'inductive risk'. Acceptance rules are special decision rules. Four outcomes: true accepted, false rejected, false accepted, true rejected. The last two are the inductive risk. Value statements have no role as evidence, but values enter the acceptance rule.
numbers: Four-cell outcome table. No numbers.
quote: The possibility of the latter two represents the inductive risk that any acceptance rule must involve.
limits: Read only as quoted in Douglas (2000), not the original essay.
agent_relevance: Gives the agent a 2x2 error table per claim (false accept vs false reject) as the data structure for a threshold.

source: Douglas (2000) Inductive Risk and Values in Science (the thesis)
finding: Douglas extends inductive risk beyond accepting a hypothesis. Non-epistemic values matter at three internal stages: choice of methodology, characterisation of data (borderline evidence), and interpretation of results. Values act indirectly, as weights on the consequences of error, not as evidence.
numbers: Philosophy of Science 67(4), pp 559-579. Three internal decision points plus three accepted external roles (problem choice, use of technology, limits on methods such as human subjects).
quote: Inductive risk is the risk of error in accepting or rejecting hypotheses.
limits: Normative argument. The case study is real regulatory science but the paper does not test whether values actually changed outcomes.
agent_relevance: The agent has several places to set thresholds, not one: which test to run, how to label an ambiguous observation, how to read the result. Each needs its own error-cost stance.

source: Douglas (2000) Inductive Risk and Values in Science (dioxin rat liver slides, the three re-readings)
finding: The same Kociba (1978) female rat liver slides were read three times: 1978 original, 1980 by Squire for the EPA, 1990 by seven pathologists for a paper-industry contractor. Tumour counts fell sharply at the 1990 reading. Only the classification was redone, not the experiment.
numbers: 50 female rats per dose group (86 controls). Dose 10 ng/kg/day: total tumour livers 20/50 (1978) vs 9/50 (1990). Dose 100: 34/50 (1978) vs 18/50 (1990). Dose 1: 3/50 (1978), 8/50 (1980), 1/50 (1990). 1980 benign tumours at 100 ng: 33/47, at 10 ng: 27/50. 1990 consensus was 4 of 7 pathologists (simple majority).
quote: consensus was reached when at least four out of seven pathologists agreed
limits: Table text came from PDF extraction and is partly garbled; the control row and the 1980 total column are uncertain. The 1990 panel was commissioned by industry, which Douglas notes. All three readings still show a rise at 10 and 100 ng/kg/day against the 1 ng dose.
agent_relevance: Concrete case of a borderline-label decision where the reader's error-cost stance roughly halves the downstream count. An agent labelling ambiguous evidence should log the label rule and test how much the result depends on it.

source: Douglas (2000) Inductive Risk and Values in Science (false positive vs false negative in this case)
finding: Calling every borderline lesion benign gives few false positives and more false negatives, so risk is underestimated and regulation relaxed (Maine did this after 1990). Calling every borderline lesion malignant does the reverse: apparent risk rises and regulation is stricter than needed, with economic cost.
numbers: Standard significance is 95%, so false positives are 5% or less. Neither direction is neutral.
quote: one must decide what balance between false positives and false negatives is optimal
limits: Douglas gives no loss numbers; the right balance for dioxin studies is 'currently unclear'.
agent_relevance: Template for the cost table the agent needs: name what a false accept costs and what a false reject costs, in the domain's own terms, before choosing the threshold.

source: Douglas (2000) Inductive Risk and Values in Science (power, cost and the limit of detection)
finding: More animals would lower both error types but is very costly. So a balance must be struck, which needs an ethical judgment. A 1% excess cancer rate cannot be detected with 50 rats per group; an apparent 'threshold' may only be a limit of detection.
numbers: Typical studies use 50-100 animals per dose group. A two-year study with 200 rats (50 at each of 3 doses plus 50 controls) costs about $3 million (Graham and Rhomberg 1996). A threshold affecting 10% of animals would be detectable in a Kociba-type study.
quote: it represents a limit of detection, not a limit in the activity of dioxins
limits: Cost figure is 1990s dollars as reported by Douglas.
agent_relevance: Insight for the agent: absence of a detected effect under low power is not evidence of no effect. A no-effect conclusion needs a power check before it is accepted.

source: Douglas (2000) Inductive Risk and Values in Science (blinding as a partial answer)
finding: Blinding pathologists to dose group stops values acting directly (seeing what you want to see). But it does not remove the need to weigh error consequences, and it only helps if borderline calls are spread evenly across groups.
limits: Douglas says blinding is still good practice and should not be dropped.
agent_relevance: Separates two jobs: hide the hoped-for answer from the labeller (direct role, bad) but keep the stated error-cost weighting (indirect role, needed).

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Scientific Objectivity (inductive risk section)
finding: Gives the standard map of the debate: Rudner (1953) argument; Hempel (1965) modified version separating confirmation from acceptance; Jeffrey (1956) and Levi (1960) replies; Douglas (2000) extension to the whole inquiry; Douglas (2009) direct vs indirect roles; Steele and Winsberg (2012) on value-laden uncertainty; Betz (2013) on hedged statements; Neyman-Pearson framing.
numbers: No numbers. Page text was read through a fetch tool that returned a summary of the first 100000 of 141853 characters.
limits: Secondary source. Wald is not mentioned there. Read via a fetch summary, not as raw text, so no verbatim quotes.
agent_relevance: Good index of which objections the agent design should answer: probability reports are also value-laden (Steele), but hedged reporting can avoid the problem (Betz).

source: Jeffrey (1956) Valuation and Acceptance of Scientific Hypotheses, as reported in SEP and Douglas (2000)
finding: Jeffrey's reply: general theories have no single use, so the scientist cannot tailor acceptance to consequences. The scientist should give probabilities and not accept or reject.
limits: Read only as reported in SEP and Douglas (2000), where a footnote credits Jeffrey with the point that theory is not tied to one use.
agent_relevance: Splits two agent roles: an estimator that outputs a probability, and a decider that applies a cost threshold. This supports a code-side decision: the model supplies the probability, the program applies the cost.

source: Levi (1960) Must the scientist make value judgments, as reported in SEP and Henschen (2021)
finding: Levi's reply: community standards (for example the 5% significance level) fix when a claim counts as established. Also the argument blurs deciding what to do and deciding what to believe. Only action needs values.
numbers: Example standard: reject when significance falls below 5%.
limits: Read only via secondary descriptions. Douglas (2000) dates the Levi reference as 1962.
agent_relevance: Belief state and action state should be kept apart. The threshold for committing an answer (action) can use cost, while the stored belief should not be bent by hoped-for outcomes.

source: Henschen (2021) How strong is the argument from inductive risk? Euro J Phil Sci
finding: Argues that confidence in the inductive risk argument is overrated. Defenders (Douglas, Wilholt) have not answered Jeffrey's objection (give probabilities only) or Levi's objection (action versus belief).
limits: Only the abstract page was read, through a fetch summary, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: The founding argument is contested. The agent should adopt the cost-threshold idea for actions, which both sides allow, and not rely on the stronger claim about belief.

source: Dressel (2022) Inductive risk: does it really refute value-freedom? Theoria 37(2)
finding: Builds an idealised Bayesian model. The agent performs action D (for example uses a model) iff p exceeds threshold t. t is the probability where the total expected utilities of 'perform D' and 'not perform D' are equal. Outcomes split into first-order (truth, error, missed truth, averted error) and second-order (consequences for science and for society). Concludes the perfect scientist need not descriptively use non-epistemic values, but normatively should in some cases.
numbers: Four first-order outcomes. A trade-off parameter T between 0 and 1 weights scientific against extra-scientific utility; T = 1 gives science only. The decision algorithm is his Table 1.
quote: The classic answer is that the threshold depends on how bad the consequences of error would be.
limits: Binary decisions and single choices only. Dressel says it could extend to accept/reject/suspend. Utility maximisation is assumed and he notes it is not the only candidate.
agent_relevance: Closest formal model to a coded threshold. In the simple binary case with zero utility for correct outcomes, t = C_fp / (C_fp + C_fn). A concrete formula the agent can run.

source: Tunc and Tunc (2025 draft) Is the value-free ideal of science untenable? Part I: Inductive risk
finding: Attacks two premises of the argument: epistemic insufficiency (internal standards cannot set thresholds) and legitimate value-encroachment. Claims thresholds are not set arbitrarily in practice, that value-laden thresholds can end debates too early, and that a meta-criterion problem leads to wishful thinking and Mannheim-style paradoxes.
numbers: No empirical numbers. 11,335 words, draft dated 21 April 2025, preprint.
limits: Pre-print, not peer reviewed; the authors ask not to be quoted directly. Part of an ongoing exchange. I read the abstract and opening only.
agent_relevance: Names a real risk for the agent: letting cost-of-error pull the stated probability (wishful thinking). Keep cost in the decision step, not in the belief step.

source: Manski (2026) Coping with Inductive Risk When Theories are Underdetermined: Decision Making with Partial Identification (critique of the 5% / 10-20% convention)
finding: Standard testing fixes Type I error at 5% and accepts Type II error of 10-20%, with no rationale. It also ignores the size of the loss. Manski and Tetenov (2016) propose minimax regret instead.
numbers: Conventional 5% Type I vs 10-20% Type II. Three stated flaws: asymmetric error rates, no loss magnitudes, only two options.
quote: The theory of hypothesis testing gives no rationale for use of these error probabilities.
limits: Economics view, argued by example, with no new experiment in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Replace a fixed 'accept at 0.95 confidence' with a rule that uses loss size. The usual default is a convention, not a derivation.

source: Manski (2026) Coping with Inductive Risk When Theories are Underdetermined: Decision Making with Partial Identification (regret as the measure of inductive risk)
finding: In Wald's decision theory, regret equals the chance of choosing wrongly times the loss when wrong: type I probability times loss of choosing B when A is better, and type II probability times loss of choosing A when B is better. This treats both errors symmetrically and uses loss size. Manski argues it is what Douglas (2000) asked for.
numbers: Regret = P(error) x welfare loss for each state. Wald (1950) statistical decision functions; Manski (2007, ch 12) proof.
limits: Needs a loss function and a state space, which the agent may not have. The paper is dated Feb 2026, revised April 2026.
agent_relevance: A usable formula for the agent: rank options by expected regret, not by a probability cutoff.

source: Manski (2026) Coping with Inductive Risk When Theories are Underdetermined: Decision Making with Partial Identification (do not have to accept or reject)
finding: Rudner and Hempel assumed the only options are accept or reject. Manski says that when evidence fits several hypotheses, the decision maker need not pick one. Under partial identification, minimax regret can still give a policy choice without accepting a theory.
numbers: Maximin and minimax regret differ; minimax regret can diversify across treatments in his two-treatment example.
quote: a decision maker need not accept one and reject the others
limits: Theoretical argument with examples from treatment choice. Not tested on language models.
agent_relevance: Supports a third state besides accept and reject: act under ambiguity, hedge or split, or ask. Fits G6 (never abstain on the first pass) by acting on a robust choice.

source: Angelopoulos, Bates, Fisch, Lei, Schuster (2022, v4 2025) Conformal Risk Control
finding: Extends conformal prediction to control the expected value of any monotone loss. The user picks the loss and a tolerance alpha, and the method picks the threshold so that expected loss is at most alpha, with a finite-sample guarantee.
numbers: Theorem 1: E[L_{n+1}] <= alpha. Tumour segmentation: false-negative-rate target 0.1, achieved mean 0.0987, sd 0.0114 over 1000 random splits; n=1000 calibration, 781 validation images. Tight up to an O(1/n) factor.
limits: Needs exchangeable data and a monotone loss. The loss must be chosen by a person, so the value choice moves into the loss and alpha rather than disappearing.
agent_relevance: Inductive risk made operational: a person sets the cost weighting, the method sets the threshold. Candidate for a calibrated accept gate in code.

source: Angelopoulos, Bates, Candes, Jordan, Lei (2021/2022) Learn then Test
finding: Recasts picking a risk-controlling threshold as multiple hypothesis testing, giving finite-sample guarantees for any model and any data distribution, without refitting.
numbers: Examples include false discovery rate control in multilabel classification and intersection-over-union control; guarantees are finite-sample.
limits: Assumes calibration data match deployment. Abstract and method opening read, not every experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives the agent a way to choose a threshold per task with a stated error rate, if a labelled calibration set exists.

source: Mohri and Hashimoto (2024) Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
finding: Treats correctness of an LM output as an uncertainty problem. Conformal prediction becomes a back-off algorithm: remove the least certain sub-claims until the output meets a user-set correctness target.
numbers: Base GPT-4 correctness to guaranteed level: FActScore 30% to 80%, NaturalQuestions 78% to 93%, MATH 75% to 95%. Targets of 80-90% were met while keeping most sub-claims. Empirical factuality varied with sd 0.09 across small calibration sets.
limits: Guarantee is marginal over calibration draws, so a small calibration set gives a wide spread (sd 0.09). Needs human-annotated samples for calibration. Correctness is entailment-based.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of an error-rate threshold. The user's tolerance alpha plays the role of the value judgment. The trade is fewer claims for more correctness, the same trade Rudner described.

source: Quach, Fisch, Schuster et al. (2024) Conformal Language Modeling, ICLR 2024
finding: Calibrates a stopping rule for sampling and a rejection rule for dropping low-quality candidates, so the output set contains at least one acceptable response with a stated probability.
numbers: Two tolerance parameters: alpha for error and delta for calibration sensitivity. Tasks: open-domain QA, summarisation, radiology report generation. The MAX scoring function beat SUM and FIRST-K on sample efficiency.
limits: I read the method and set-up, not every table. Quality depends on a score that is itself learned from a calibration set.
agent_relevance: Shows an agent can draw samples until a calibrated confidence target is met, and stop. The target is the cost-of-error setting.

source: BlackRock authors (2024) How to Choose a Threshold for an Evaluation Metric for Large Language Models, arXiv 2412.12148
finding: Recipe adapted from model risk management in finance for choosing a threshold on an LLM metric such as faithfulness. Methods: Z-score, kernel density, empirical recall, AUC-ROC and conformal prediction. Stakeholders must say how much Type I and Type II error they accept.
numbers: Tested on HaluBench (about 15K question, context, answer triplets with human labels) and open-source metrics (Uptrain, DeepEval, RAGAS). Tables report thresholds at 80-99% confidence; I do not quote cell values because the PDF extraction of the tables is garbled.
quote: An overly lenient threshold may result in a high number of false positives
limits: The text says the cost trade-off is left to stakeholders. Author list not checked. Result tables were not read reliably.
agent_relevance: Shows industry already treats LLM thresholds as an error-cost decision made by people. Supports keeping the threshold a visible parameter.

source: Rudner (1953) (the statistical-inference step, citing Rosander 1951 and Neyman 1950)
finding: Rudner ties the argument to statistics. Choosing a significance level is choosing how often you will accept a false hypothesis. The usual levels have no rigid theoretical justification. Neyman is cited for the point that which of the two errors matters more is a subjective matter.
numbers: Common levels: 1 percent, 5 percent and 0.3 of one percent. At the 5 percent level, a false hypothesis is accepted about one time in twenty over the long run.
quote: There is nothing sacred about these three values
limits: Rudner quotes Rosander (1951) for the levels and Neyman (1950) for the subjective-matter remark; I did not read those books.
agent_relevance: Confirms a default confidence cut-off (for example 0.95) is an inherited convention. The agent should treat it as a tunable setting tied to error cost.
